hints: Look at the equation for reaction A and notice what happens to the water molecule as sucrose splits into two smaller sugars.
walkthrough:
Spot the role of water**
Look at $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow$ glucose + fructose. One large molecule is split into two smaller molecules by adding a water molecule across the linking bond. Whenever water is used in this way to break a molecule apart, we call it hydrolysis.

hints: Count the C, H and O atoms in the displayed structures of glucose and fructose to compare their molecular formulae.
Compare where the $\text{C=O}$ carbonyl group sits in each chain, at the end of the chain or in the middle of the chain.
walkthrough:
Check the molecular formula first**
Count carefully from the structures. Both glucose and fructose contain 6 carbons, 12 hydrogens and 6 oxygens, so both are $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$. Structural isomers must share the same molecular formula, so this is your first essential point.

Find the difference in connectivity**
Now look at how those atoms are joined. In glucose the $\text{C=O}$ is at carbon 1 as $\text{CHO}$, an aldehyde group at the end of the chain. In fructose the $\text{C=O}$ is at carbon 2 as $\text{C(=O)CH}_2\text{OH}$, a ketone group in the middle of the chain. Same atoms, different order of bonding, so they are structural isomers with different functional groups.

Final answer: Both have molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$.
Same atoms but arranged differently: glucose has the carbonyl group at the end of the chain (aldehyde) whereas fructose has the carbonyl group in the middle of the chain (ketone).

hints: Recall how an enzyme as a catalyst changes the reaction pathway and what this does to the activation energy compared with the uncatalysed route.
walkthrough:
Remember what an enzyme does**
Reaction B uses an enzyme and reaction A does not. An enzyme provides an alternative route with a lower activation energy, so $E_a$ for B is lower. Since $E_a$ for B is $+29 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$, $E_a$ for A without the enzyme must be larger, any value greater than $+29 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Final answer: Any value more than $+29 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ for reaction A.

hints: Think about whether a catalyst changes the starting reactants, the final products, or only the route between them.
walkthrough:
Separate $E_a$ from $\Delta H$**
Enthalpy change depends only on the energy of reactants and products: $\Delta H = H(\text{products}) - H(\text{reactants})$. A catalyst lowers the top of the hump but does not change the start or finish levels. So $\Delta H$ for B is identical to A, $-14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

hints: Decide whether reactants are higher or lower than products for an exothermic change of $-14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and how to show $\Delta H$ as a vertical arrow.
Recall how to show activation energy as the vertical distance from reactants up to the top of the hump for reaction B.
walkthrough:
Draw the exothermic shape**
Start with labelled axes, energy on the y axis and progress of reaction on the x axis. Draw a horizontal line for reactants, then a smooth hump, then a lower horizontal line for products. Because $\Delta H$ is negative, products must sit lower than reactants.

Label the two energy gaps**
Draw a vertical arrow pointing down from reactants to products and label it $\Delta H = -14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. Draw a second vertical arrow pointing up from reactants to the very top of the hump and label it $E_a = +29 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$. That top arrow is the barrier the enzyme has already lowered.

Final answer: Exothermic profile with reactants level above products level.
$\Delta H = -14 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ labelled as drop from reactants to products.
$E_a = +29 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ labelled as rise from reactants to peak of hump.

hints: Focus on the amount of sucrose the definition refers to, one mole, not one gram.
Think about the exact wording needed for burning, complete reaction and the supply of oxygen.
walkthrough:
Pin down the amount**
Enthalpy change of combustion is always quoted per mole of fuel burned. So begin with: when 1 mole of sucrose reacts.

Pin down the reaction type**
Combustion means burning in oxygen to give $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. For the standard definition you must state complete combustion in excess oxygen or air, so no CO or soot remains. Together this gives: the enthalpy change when 1 mole of sucrose burns completely in excess oxygen.
Final answer: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of sucrose burns completely in excess oxygen.

hints: Start with $q = mc\Delta T$ for the water, using $m = 250 \text{ g}$, $c = 4.18 \text{ J g}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 40.7 - 25.0$.
Convert $1.00 \text{ g}$ of sucrose to moles using $M_r$ of sucrose $= 342$.
Scale the heat released by $1.00 \text{ g}$ up to the heat released by one mole and remember the sign for an exothermic combustion.
walkthrough:
Find the heat taken up by the water**
Use $$q = mc\Delta T$$ where $m$ is the mass of water heated. Here $$q = 250 \times 4.18 \times (40.7 - 25.0)$$ $$q = 250 \times 4.18 \times 15.7 = 16406.5 \text{ J}$$ This is the energy released by burning $1.00 \text{ g}$ of sucrose, about $16.4 \text{ kJ g}^{-1}$.

Convert grams of sucrose to moles**
$M_r$ of $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{22}\text{O}_{11} = 342$. So $$\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r} = \frac{1.00}{342} = 0.002924 \text{ mol}$$ You have heated the water with only this tiny number of moles.

Scale to one mole and add the sign**
Divide energy per gram by moles per gram: $$\Delta H_c = -\frac{16406.5}{0.002924} = -5610000 \text{ J mol}^{-1}$$ Convert J to kJ: $$\Delta H_c = -5610 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Negative because combustion is exothermic, heat is released. Give to 3 significant figures to match the data.

Final answer: $q = mc\Delta T = 250 \times 4.18 \times (40.7 - 25.0) = 16406.5 \text{ J}$ released by $1.00 \text{ g}$
Moles sucrose in $1.00 \text{ g} = 1.00/342 = 0.002924 \text{ mol}$
$\Delta H_c = -16406.5 / 0.002924 / 1000 = -5610 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ (3 s.f.)
